ai.definition: Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) is a non-invasive neuroimaging technique that measures brain activity by detecting changes in blood flow. It provides detailed images of the brain's structure and can also reveal which areas are active during certain tasks or states.
ai.howItWorks: fMRI works by using strong magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of the brain. When a particular area of the brain is active, there is an increase in blood flow to that region, which fMRI can detect as changes in signal intensity. This allows researchers and clinicians to map brain activity non-invasively.
ai.problemSolved: fMRI addresses the challenge of understanding how different regions of the brain function during various tasks or states without requiring invasive procedures like surgery.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves complex engineering, including the assembly of large MRI machines with precise magnetic field generation and radio frequency transmission capabilities. The components are typically sourced from specialized suppliers worldwide.
ai.buildProcess: fMRI machines are built in a controlled environment to ensure accuracy and safety. The process includes assembly, calibration, and extensive testing before deployment in clinical or research settings.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high cost of machine acquisition, ongoing maintenance, and the need for highly trained personnel to operate and interpret results. Additional costs come from the specialized software required for data analysis.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as fMRI continues to be refined and integrated into various applications, including clinical diagnostics and research studies.
ai.regulation: fMRI devices are regulated by agencies such as the FDA in the United States. Compliance with safety standards and performance criteria is mandatory for market entry.
ai.risks: Risks include potential radiation exposure from the strong magnetic fields (though minimal), patient contraindications, and the complexity of data interpretation which can lead to misdiagnosis or incorrect conclusions.
ai.profitability: Profitability varies widely depending on the application. Clinical use in hospitals and research institutions provides steady revenue streams, while consumer applications may struggle due to lower demand and higher costs.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development focuses on improving resolution, reducing scan times, and enhancing data analysis techniques to better understand brain function and connectivity.

glossary.def: The change in blood flow that fMRI detects to indicate brain activity.

subsystems.name: Superconducting main magnet
subsystems.role: creates the strong, uniform static field that polarises hydrogen nuclei in the brain.

subsystems.name: Gradient coils
subsystems.role: add small, rapidly switched fields that encode spatial position, which is what makes an image possible.
parts: x, y, z gradient coil sets

subsystems.name: Radio-frequency coils
subsystems.role: transmit pulses that tip nuclear spins and receive the faint signal back.

subsystems.name: Pulse sequence and reconstruction
subsystems.role: controls the timing of gradients and RF, then turns raw signals into images.

subsystems.name: Stimulus and response system
subsystems.role: presents tasks and records behaviour during scanning.

subsystems.name: Analysis pipeline
subsystems.role: turns a time series of images into maps of brain activity.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the site
buildSteps.detail: A magnetically shielded room with a radio-frequency cage blocks external interference, and the floor is built to carry the magnet's weight.

buildSteps.title: Wind the magnet
buildSteps.detail: Superconducting wire is wound into coils, clamped against the enormous magnetic forces, and sealed inside a cryostat.

buildSteps.title: Cool down
buildSteps.detail: The magnet is cooled with liquid helium to a few kelvin, where the wire loses all resistance and can hold a persistent current.

buildSteps.title: Fit gradients and shims
buildSteps.detail: Gradient coils are installed inside the bore and shim coils correct the field to a uniformity of a few parts per million.

buildSteps.title: Add RF coils
buildSteps.detail: A transmit coil and a close-fitting receive array go around the head, since signal falls off steeply with distance.

buildSteps.title: Tune the sequence
buildSteps.detail: Engineers set echo time and repetition time so the sequence is sensitive to the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal, then test it on phantoms and volunteers.

buildSteps.title: Scan the subject
buildSteps.detail: A person performs a task while the scanner collects one brain volume every one to two seconds.

buildSteps.title: Preprocess and model
buildSteps.detail: Images are corrected for head motion and slice timing, aligned to anatomy, and fitted with a statistical model to produce activation maps.

prerequisites.why: the static field of 1.5–7 T cannot be produced by resistive magnets at acceptable power.
echo-planar imaging needs gradients that switch in under a millisecond to read a whole volume quickly.

prerequisites.tech: Multi-channel receive arrays and parallel imaging
prerequisites.why: they shorten scan time and improve signal near the cortex.
thousands of images per run must be reconstructed and corrected in real time or near it.

prerequisites.tech: A validated model of neurovascular coupling
prerequisites.why: BOLD is an indirect, slow proxy for neural activity, so its interpretation remains an active research question.

pathway.milestone: 3 T scanners as the workhorse, with 7 T systems used in research and some clinical settings
pathway.unlocks: routine mapping of sensory, motor and language areas before surgery, plus cognitive research.

pathway.milestone: faster acquisition via multiband and MR encephalography-style sequences
pathway.unlocks: tracking activity closer to the speed at which the brain actually works.

pathway.milestone: wider use of portable low-field scanners
pathway.unlocks: bedside and remote imaging, though BOLD sensitivity at low field is limited.

pathway.milestone: real-time decoding and closed-loop stimulation combined with EEG or MEG
pathway.unlocks: direct, causal tests of brain circuits rather than correlation alone.
